analysis.one_liner: Requires most employers to pay workers at least 1.5 times their regular rate for working federal holidays.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring time-and-a-half pay for work on federal holidays was introduced in the Senate in February 2026 with zero cosponsors and has seen no committee action since.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal wage law requires overtime after 40 hours a week, but it does not require any extra pay for working a holiday like Thanksgiving or July 4th; holiday premium pay today depends on a union contract, a company policy, or a state law. This bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to require employers covered by that law to pay anyone who works on a federal holiday at least one and a half times their regular rate. It would also let workers sue for unpaid holiday pay through the same enforcement system used for unpaid minimum wage and overtime.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers who are scheduled to work on federal holidays — retail clerks, grocery and restaurant staff, hotel and warehouse workers, and hospital and other healthcare employees without union contracts guaranteeing holiday pay — would see their holiday shifts paid at 1.5 times their regular rate.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new section to the Fair Labor Standards Act barring employers from employing covered workers on a 'legal public holiday' — defined as any holiday listed in federal law — unless they are paid at least 1.5 times their regular rate for that work.

It treats unpaid holiday pay like unpaid minimum wage and overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act's enforcement provisions, allowing workers to recover it privately and the Department of Labor to enforce it.
It prevents employers from crediting holiday premium pay toward overtime obligations, so holiday pay would come on top of overtime rather than substituting for it.
It preserves any federal, state, or local holiday pay rules that are more generous than the new federal minimum, so workers in states with stronger laws do not lose anything.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in sectors that stay open on holidays — retail, food service, hospitality, warehouses, and hospitals — would bear higher labor costs on those days. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices, offset through reduced holiday staffing, or absorbed in margins.

drawbacks.text: Requiring 1.5 times pay for holiday work raises labor costs for businesses open on holidays, which may respond by paying consumers more, offering fewer holiday shifts, or absorbing the cost in tighter margins.

The requirement attaches to workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act, so salaried executive, administrative, and professional workers exempt from that law would not get the holiday premium, nor would certain rail and motor carrier employees the bill adds to an existing exemption.

Many union workers and workers in some states already receive holiday premium pay under contracts or state law, so for them the bill would change little; it mainly raises the floor for non-union workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers without a union contract or a generous state law, the bill delivers a real raise on holiday shifts, and the mechanism is the same one used to recover unpaid overtime, so it is straightforward to enforce. The costs fall on employers in holiday-opening industries and partly on consumers through prices, and salaried exempt workers are left out. On balance the bill helps a broad group of ordinary workers at a modest, focused cost to specific industries, but with zero cosponsors and no committee action, it has not moved toward becoming law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on February 12, 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat without further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Ruben Gallego introduced the Holiday Pay Act in the Senate on February 12, 2026.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, and no further actions appear in the record.
No senators have cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not advanced, nothing has changed: employers in industries open on holidays continue to owe only their existing pay obligations, and workers whose holiday pay depends on a contract or state law remain where they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, so far — no change yet

for.name: Sen. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee; no senator has joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Senate committee of jurisdiction, where the bill sits
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for consideration since it was referred on February 12, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic senator introduced the bill with no cosponsors of either party, so there is no record of cross-party support.

industries.note: These industries stay open on federal holidays and would owe 1.5 times pay to holiday workers. They could pass costs to consumers through prices or trim holiday staffing.
Holiday demand is high in food service and lodging, so holiday premium pay raises labor costs on their busiest days.
Healthcare cannot close on holidays, so facilities would pay more for holiday shifts; many already pay holiday differentials, so the effect varies by employer.

industries.industry: Unionized workplaces with existing holiday pay clauses
industries.note: Employers who already promised holiday premium pay in union contracts would owe the higher federal floor where their current terms are lower; workers in these workplaces gain little because they mostly already receive the premium.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action two months after introduction, the likely path is that the bill stays in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote, unless a cosponsor effort or a labor-committee markup changes that.
